references.text: Psalm 110:1 is the direct quotation that Jesus refers to in his argument. David calls the Messiah "my Lord" ([ref:Sal 110:1|Psalm 110:1]), which shows that the Messiah is more than just a biological descendant of David – he is David's Lord.

The parallel text in [ref:Matt 22:43-45|Matthew 22:43-45] presents the same question from Jesus: How can David call the Messiah "Lord" if the Messiah is only David's son? Matthew's version emphasizes that David spoke "in the Spirit."
The parallel text in [ref:Mark 12:37|Mark 12:37] poses the same rhetorical question: "David himself calls him Lord, how then can he be his son?" Mark adds that the crowd listened to him with delight.

Peter quotes Psalm 110:1 in his Pentecost sermon ([ref:Apg 2:34-36|Acts 2:34-36]) and confirms that David did not ascend into heaven himself, but prophesied about Jesus as Lord and Messiah, exalted to God's right hand.

Paul writes that Jesus Christ "according to the flesh is descended from David" but "according to the Spirit of holiness was declared to be the powerful Son of God" ([ref:Rom 1:3-4|Romans 1:3-4]). This illuminates the tension in Jesus' question: The Messiah is David's son according to the flesh, but far more than that – he is Lord.

In [ref:Fil 2:9-11|Philippians 2:9-11] it is confirmed that Jesus has been given the name above every name, and that "every tongue shall confess that Jesus Christ is Lord." This supports the point in Luke 20:44 that the Messiah is Lord, not only David's son.

In [ref:Åp 22:16|Revelation 22:16] Jesus calls himself "the root and offspring of David." The expression "root of David" points to him being David's origin and Lord, while "offspring" shows that he is David's descendant – a duality that corresponds to the question Jesus asks in Luke 20:44.
